title: Where Were You?
mood: One question, years late, asked in a plain room at night. The next day, the hall under five stars.

hero.alt: In the firelight small Chang'e is held against Lesley's shoulder, a tear on her cheek behind her round glasses.

segs.t: The lab was dark except for the console. Chang’e sat in front of it, Mr. Bunny at her shoulder.
The line about the coil was still open.
Lesley, the coil runs cooler now.
She opened the folder it belonged to.
Forty-three drafts like it lay there, one under another. Every one was addressed to Lesley. Every one was a single line about work.
Lesley, your visor seal is fixed.
Lesley, the third years’ suits passed inspection.
Chang’e knew the line that should have come after each. She had never once typed it.
Above the forty-three, the log ran back for years. She went up past all of them, to the one she never scrolled back to.
I’ll never forgive you, Lesley. You were not here when we needed your protection. They died because of you!
She had typed it the night of the fall, in her father’s chair. She read it once. It sounded like somebody very small.
She scrolled back down to the coil.
This morning she had told Angela about a fault in her chest.
It comes and goes,
she had said.
I can fix it in a minute.
Angela had laid a hand over the place. She did not want it fixed.
Under the line about the coil, she typed:
Where were you?
She looked at it for a long time. Mr. Bunny looked at it too.
She did not send it.
Not on a screen,
she thought.
She left it there, unsent, and took Mr. Bunny down the corridor.
Lesley’s door was not locked. It never was.
The cot stood along the wall, made, its blanket folded square. Nobody had ever slept on it.
Lesley slept in the hard chair beside it, upright, boots on. The chair faced the door, so from the doorway the first thing Chang’e saw was her face.
The rifle leaned within reach of her right hand. The new coil sat on top of it now, fitted over the old bolt.
Chang’e stood in the doorway with Mr. Bunny at her shoulder. She spoke very low.
“Big Sis, Mr. Bunny says he was lonely.”
Lesley’s right eye opened. It went to the robot, then to the girl.
“Only him?”
“Mostly him.”
Chang’e climbed onto the end of the cot nearest the chair. The cot was harder than it looked. She tucked her feet under her and took hold of one square corner of the blanket.
“Where were you?” She said it fast, before she could stop herself. “That day. I stopped being angry a long time ago. I never asked.”
Lesley did not move. Down the corridor a lamp buzzed.
“I was away on a mission,” she said at last. “I can’t tell you what it was.”
“Still?”
“Still.”
Chang’e waited.
“No radio. No letters. I switched mine off at the gate.”
“Nine days,” said Chang’e. “I counted.”
Lesley looked at her, then at the rifle.
“I came back past midnight and called the base once.” She paused. “Only hiss.”
Chang’e’s fingers stopped on the blanket.
Lesley. Lesley, come in.
Her mother had said it into the radio from her coat as they ran across the yard. The radio had only hissed back.
“The squads at the edge had nobody leading them,” said Lesley. “So I turned the dial to the Shield’s channel and took them. I left it there.”
She called us,
thought Chang’e.
Mom called her. Hiss both ways.
Lesley’s left hand lay on her knee. “Then I saw the giant walk in behind us. It was a decoy. I ran for the base.”
“You ran.”
“Halfway there, your alarm started. The giant fired first.”
Chang’e laid the night out in order, the way her father would have counted it. The alarm first. Then her mother running, the radio at her mouth.
She was already running when Mom called,
she thought.
With the dial on the Shield’s.
At the crater, the glove on that left hand had been burned through at the palm, and the palm under it raw. Chang’e had seen it. She had never asked about that either.
“I’d promised,” said Lesley. She said it flat, the way she gave casualty counts on the channel.
Chang’e let go of the blanket. She reached out and took hold of Lesley’s coat sleeve, as she had at the gate.
Lesley looked down at the small hand. She let it stay.
Chang’e did not tell her about the call.
That one she doesn’t need.
“Why the base?” she asked instead.
Lesley took longer over that one. “I never found out.”
“You could have told me.”
“You never asked.”
“I just did.”
“Yes.”
Chang’e kept hold of the sleeve. With her other hand she found a loose thread in the blanket’s corner. The square fold had come undone.
“If you had a reason,” she said, “then who’s left?”
Lesley waited.
“The giant. And Mom and Dad.” She pulled at the thread. “They pushed me clear. I had my eyes shut.”
The night of the fall she had typed
I had my eyes
under the letter, and deleted it.
She wound the thread round her finger.
“As long as it was your fault, it wasn’t theirs. Or mine.”
Mr. Bunny sank down onto the blanket beside her and settled there.
Lesley’s left hand closed on her knee.
“They chose,” she said, and nothing more.
Chang’e wound the thread tighter. Two white coats had stood between her and the light, their backs to her, and taken a step toward it.
My eyes were open for that part,
she thought.
After a while she looked up at the field roster over the cot. Her name had never been on it.
“And the rotation,” she said. “At the door today.”
Lesley was quiet so long that Mr. Bunny’s screen dimmed, the way it did when nobody needed him.
“The last time I was away, they died.”
Lesley turned her head and looked at her. “In the field, I can’t see you.”
Chang’e’s hand tightened on the sleeve.
“That’s a reason,” she said. “The first one you ever gave me.”
“It’s the one I have.”
“It’s not a good one.”
“No.”
“Put me on the rotation.”
“No.”
Chang’e laughed once, through her nose. “Good. Now I know what I’m arguing with.”
Her eyes went to Mr. Bunny, dim on the blanket, then to the thread on her finger.
“I put Angela on a list this morning. I can’t see inside her, so she stays on checks.” She unwound the thread. “It’s the same thing. I know it’s the same. I did it anyway.”
Lesley looked at her a long moment. “Yes.”
Chang’e looked past her at the rifle, the bright coil over the old bolt.
“Why keep the old action?”
Lesley’s hand went to the bolt and rested there. “You built it.”
The bolt sat under Lesley’s fingers. Chang’e had filed it smooth herself, back at the base, and then filed it again.
Behind her glasses, the bolt went blurred.
Then she leaned sideways until her head rested against Lesley’s arm. The sleeve smelled of gun oil. In a minute she was asleep.
The Academy hall. The next day.

Rows of chairs faced an altar, and five great stars stood above it. A tall window threw colored light across the floor. Chang’e stood at the back with Mr. Bunny. A director could stand where she liked.
Under the boards lay the crater. She had driven this hall’s first stake into it herself.

In front stood four girls in combat suits. Layla and Fanny were shoulder to shoulder, not arguing. Ruby had her scythe grounded and her eyes on the floor in front of Lesley’s boots. Angela had the doll clipped at her hip. The other students stood along the walls in uniform.
Lesley stood before the four with her hands behind her back. “Ruby, Angela: you are Aspirants as of today. The four of you stand together.”

At dawn Chang’e had woken on the cot, her head still against Lesley’s arm. Lesley sat exactly as straight as she had in the night. Under her breath, to the door, she was saying what came next. Twice. Chang’e had kept her eyes shut and let her.
Lesley’s eye went along the four of them, one by one.
“We still don’t fully understand our own power. But by trusting each other, we can gain limitless strength.”
On those last words, Chang’e looked to the door.

Vexana waited by the door in her school uniform, arms folded. Guinevere, also in uniform, saw her from along the wall and waved with her whole arm. A chibi keychain, a tiny big-headed doll, swung at each girl’s belt. Guinevere wore a black-haired Vexana. Vexana wore a pink-haired Guinevere.

media.alt: In the Academy hall under tall colored windows and great stars, black-haired Vexana in school uniform waits by the door while Guinevere waves her whole arm, Lesley and four girls far off at the altar; then Vexana looks back over her shoulder, and Guinevere grins with her arm up.

segs.t: The speech ended. In front, Layla turned around. Guinevere swung the same wave at her.
Then the hall emptied. The students went out past Chang’e in twos.
Lesley came down the aisle.
Chang’e reached back for a sleeve without looking, as she had in this hall yesterday. Her fingers closed on nothing. Lesley had already stopped beside her. Nobody had towed her there.
Chang’e put the hand in her coat pocket. Together they watched the door.
Guinevere came along the wall last. On her way past the door, she took a fistful of Vexana’s sleeve and towed her out into the light.
